title: Miketz: guilt remembers (Genesis 42:21)
hookLine: years later the brothers say "We are verily guilty concerning our brother"

cards: Something you did at fourteen. A cruel thing you said to a kid at school. You haven't thought about it in years.
Then one day, something small, a song, a name, a face in a crowd, and it's right there again, as sharp as the day it happened. Famine has come, just as Joseph said.
In Canaan, Jacob sends ten of his sons down to Egypt to buy grain. They stand before the governor of Egypt and bow low. They don't recognize him.

teach.b: Joseph speaks to them harshly, through an interpreter. You're spies, come to find the weak spots in our land. They protest: we're honest men, twelve brothers, sons of one father.

teach.h: ONE OF US IS NO MORE.
teach.b: The youngest is at home with our father, and one is no more. Joseph holds them in custody for three days. Then: one of you stays in prison, the rest take grain home, and bring me your youngest brother.
Right there in front of him, the brothers start talking to each other in Hebrew, thinking the Egyptian can't understand.
And what comes out, more than twenty years after the pit, is this, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "We are verily guilty concerning our brother."

teach.h: WE SAW HIS DISTRESS, AND WOULD NOT HEAR.
teach.b: We saw the distress of his soul when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen. That's why this distress has come on us. Notice what they remember.
Not just the act. His begging. Back at the pit, the Torah never told us Joseph pleaded with them.
We learn it only now, from their memory. Guilt kept a detail the story itself left out. Reuben adds: didn't I tell you not to sin against the boy?
And Joseph, who understands every word, turns away from them and weeps. Their words, aval ashemim anachnu, are where their teshuvah, their turning back, begins.
The key word, ashem, guilty, echoes in the confession Jews say on Yom Kippur, together, out loud: ashamnu, we have been guilty. Guilt remembers. And remembering is where repair begins.

how: On Yom Kippur, Jews confess together in the plural, beginning ashamnu, we have been guilty, and Jewish teaching on teshuvah includes naming the wrong aloud and seeking to repair it.

games.q: who did what in Egypt — tap the pairs.
p: we have been guilty, on Yom Kippur

s: the brothers recognized Joseph right away
he recognized them; they didn't recognize him.

games.q: you're one of the brothers. the governor of Egypt accuses you of spying and keeps one of you in prison. what goes through your mind?
o: this is because of what we did to our brother.
games.why: they said, we are verily guilty concerning our brother: we saw his distress and would not hear.

practice: Let one old thing come up, something you did or didn't do that still stings, and don't argue with it or drown in it. Name it quietly, the way the brothers did: I did this; I saw, and didn't listen.
If you pray, you can bring it to God; then ask whether there's anything, even small, you could do to repair it.

wordCard.voice: Miketz. At the end: the portion where, years later, the brothers finally say out loud, we are verily guilty concerning our brother.
